planting.note: Root dormant hardwood cuttings or plant container stock in early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil along a shaded streambank or boggy woodland site; this boreal currant needs cool roots and steady moisture to establish.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; northern black currant is a cold-climate boreal native found along streambanks, swamp margins, and wet conifer woods from Alaska and Canada south into the northern Rockies and Great Lakes states. White, saucer-shaped flowers in spring give way to small black berries with a distinctly resinous, musky aroma that most people find too strong for fresh eating but that mellow into usable jelly and syrup when cooked with sugar. Like its relatives, it is one of the more shade-tolerant fruiting shrubs available, making it valuable for the shadiest, coldest corners of a food forest where little else fruits, but it is an alternate host for white pine blister rust and should not be planted near susceptible white pines. Mulch heavily and keep the root zone from drying out, since it struggles in hot or dry conditions outside its native cold-wet habitat.
sources: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring into well-drained, humus-rich soil at a partly shaded woodland edge; this northern native gooseberry tolerates cold, rocky, and lean sites better than cultivated gooseberries.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil at a shaded to partly sunny woodland edge or thicket margin; Canadian gooseberry is a low, spiny-caned native ranging across boreal and northern Great Plains Canada into the adjacent northern United States, often growing in rocky woods, lakeshores, and forest margins too cold or lean for most cultivated fruit. Small greenish-white flowers in spring ripen into smooth, dark purple-to-black berries that are tart but pleasant eaten fresh when fully ripe or cooked into jam. It is closely related to the cultivated American gooseberry (Ribes hirtellum) but is hardier and more shade-tolerant, serving as a tough, low-input option for the colder or shadier fringes of a food forest. Give it room to form a loose, suckering thicket and avoid heavy pruning, since fruit forms on older wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container stock in fall or early spring into cool, moist, duff-rich soil under a closed canopy; this is one of the most shade-tolerant currants and can be used as a low spreading groundcover beneath trees.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, duff-rich soil in partial to deep shade; trailing black currant is a low, sprawling Pacific coastal native found from Alaska south through British Columbia into the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, typically growing as groundcover in the deep shade of old-growth and second-growth conifer forest understory. Loose, drooping clusters of small purple-black, glandular-bristly berries ripen in summer and are edible fresh or cooked, with a mild, slightly resinous flavor milder than its upright relative stink currant. Because it spreads along the ground and tolerates very low light, it works well as a shaded woodland-floor edible groundcover in a food forest where upright shrubs would struggle, though it needs consistent moisture and cool summer conditions to perform well. Avoid planting near susceptible white pines, as Ribes species can host white pine blister rust.

planting.note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in fall into well-drained woodland soil at a partly shaded forest edge or beneath an open tree canopy; this West Coast native blooms very early, so site it where late frosts are less likely to catch the flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained woodland soil at a partly shaded forest edge or beneath an open canopy; gummy gooseberry is a spiny-stemmed Pacific Northwest native found from southwest British Columbia through Washington and Oregon into northern California, typically growing in dry-to-moist coniferous forest understory and clearings. Its striking deep red-and-white flowers open very early in spring, among the first native shrubs to bloom, and are a key early nectar source for hummingbirds before most other food-forest plants have leafed out. The sticky, bristly purple-black berries that follow are tart but good fresh or cooked once fully ripe. Once established it tolerates summer dry shade better than most fruiting shrubs, making it a useful choice for the drier, shadier margins of a Pacific coastal food forest.
